title: Social class and respect for early musicians
summary: Discussion of the social class of early musicians, subscription balls versus brawls, and respect for musicians.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: This is Reel 2, Henry Command, February 13th, 1963. We were talking there about the white musicians and how you had their replacements at the French opera. And what I was really getting at was in the early jazz days, and I don't know how much we know about that, but judging from the memories of people like Jack Lang, which is maybe even pre-jazz as we know it.
What does he go back to, Dick, about the 1890s?

No, before that. You see, he got his drums when they broke down the Cotton Exposition. He got his first real set of drums, but he had kids that he would play on toy instruments before that. He was born in 1873. So the thing that interested me and the early white bands that I hear about, I wonder what kind of social class they came from. Musicians, you're talking

about playing at the opera, would they be accepted? Yes, they were even very much respected, the musicians in the opera. Now, social class... You see, there wasn't such a strong distinction between the classical musicians. The musician who played in the French opera also played for dancing. Sometimes the whole French opera orchestra played for a really fine, fine gala dance. But more often, they went out as leaders of very smaller groups in all of these dance halls. One time there were always an enormous number of dance halls. And it added a kind of to build their dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear what they called vaudeville, which might be a whole lot lighter. And even when they played opera, they mixed it with other entertainment. Between the acts there might be sword swallowing or tightrope walking or dancing. They called it rope dancing. They had duels. They had acrobats. They had demonstrations of all kinds. They just mixed the entertainment in together. There wasn't very much of a divorce along class lines of high class and low class. Now, among the dances, there were, of course, all kinds of classes there. And some people, and a great many people, in an endeavor to keep their dances less public and more refined, had strictly private subscription dances where everyone had to sign up for ten or twelve balls in advance for season. They'd know the finances were there that way. And they'd have a series of ten or twelve subscription balls, as they called them. And you can find a class level in advances every step of the way, down to what were really brawls, mixed color, whites and negroes of both sexes all mixing it together in what must have been a pretty wild night. After the war, there I don't have first-hand research. I can't say any more broadly than you can there. That's one of the things that I hope to get to. And it's a good question to raise for that period. It needs to be answered to find out what the social status of a musician was actually here, after the war. In some ways, one would think that maybe he had a better position than the musician in many other American cities. Certainly, we know the negro musicians were idolized, if we can believe, these accounts by their own people. They say that Bolden was such a great hero. And the military band tradition was certainly very, very strong here. And don't forget that after the war, in the United States as a whole, you began to get the emergence of the Symphony Orchestra, and this carried with it a good deal of respect. You had these great military bands, like the one from Boston, I forget his name, Pat, it's an Irish name. Gilmore. And that band played here, by the way, in New Orleans, at the time when he had all those cannon wired up to shoot off together in the overture of 1812 and everything, something like a hundred cannon wired up to go off together. And they had a huge band here. So it's not very long before you begin to get the, well, Seuss's band and the American band in general. By the 1890s, you're in full swing with band concerts in the park. And like, so I don't know, I don't know.

I can imagine that the status of a musician didn't drop too far. But still, it wasn't so much frowning upon it socially. I wouldn't want to leave that impression. When the white male of a New Orleans family didn't learn music, I think it was just simply that this wasn't a good enough perfection financially. There was more money to be made in a whole lot of other things than there was to be made in music as a career.
